seeds.goal: You can write a 120–150 word letter that describes a problem with a product or a service calmly and demands a specific solution: a refund, a replacement or a repair.
seeds.why: An order arrives broken, an airline loses your luggage, a course starts three weeks late. Companies answer letters, and a calm letter with a clear demand is answered faster than an angry message in a chat.
seeds.ex: Timur bought a phone from a British online shop. It died after three days. His 140-word letter got him a new phone and an apology in a week.
seeds.read: Read the letter and find one thing: what exactly does Timur want the shop to do, and in which sentence does he say it?
seeds.task: Write a letter of complaint (120–150 words) about wireless headphones you bought online: one earphone does not charge, delivery was ten days late, and support has not answered for a week. Say what you bought and when, describe two problems, say what you have already done, demand a solution and give a deadline.
model: Say why you are writing in the first sentence
I am writing to complain about a mobile phone which I bought from your online shop on 3 March.
Although the delivery was fast, the phone has not worked properly since the first day.
The phone switches off after ten minutes, and the charger becomes extremely hot, which I find unacceptable for a new device.
Say what you have already tried
I contacted your support team twice; however, I have not received any reply.
I would therefore be grateful if you could replace the phone or give me a full refund.
I have attached a copy of the receipt and a photograph of the charger.
Set a deadline and sign off
I look forward to hearing from you within seven days. Yours faithfully, Timur Aliyev.
phr: I am writing to complain about …
I am writing with regard to the order I placed on …
Unfortunately, the product does not work properly.
Өкінішке қарай, тауар дұрыс жұмыс істемейді.
Despite my two emails, nobody has replied.
Несмотря на два письма, никто не ответил.
Екі хатыма қарамастан, ешкім жауап берген жоқ.
I would be grateful if you could refund my money.
Буду признателен, если вы вернёте деньги.
I would like to request a full refund.
Я хотел бы запросить полный возврат.
I look forward to hearing from you.
sent: I am writing to complain about a faulty laptop.
The delivery was two weeks late.
I have already contacted your support team.
Unfortunately, the screen stopped working after three days.
I would be grateful if you could refund my money.
The staff in your shop were extremely rude.
I look forward to hearing from you soon.
This situation is completely unacceptable for a new product.
The charger which came with the phone became very hot.
I have attached a copy of the receipt.
topics: It stopped charging after four days, the screen flickers and the sound disappears in headphones.
I am writing to describe the problems with the device.
I sent an email on 12 May and another on 19 May, and I called three times.
I have tried to contact you several times.
Because of the delay I had to buy another laptop and I missed two paid lessons.

seeds.sub: How to demand a solution politely

seeds.goal: You can write to a school, a hostel or a future employer: state your business, give the facts they need, ask your questions and close correctly.
seeds.why: Semi-formal is the register of most real adult writing. Too friendly and you look careless; too formal and you look like a robot.
seeds.ex: Aigerim wrote to a summer academy about accommodation. Her letter was forwarded to the housing office unchanged.
seeds.read: Read the letter and find one thing: what two questions does Aigerim need answered?
seeds.task: Write a semi-formal letter (120–150 words) to a summer school you have been accepted to: introduce yourself, confirm your place, give your arrival details, ask two practical questions and close politely.
model: I am writing to confirm my place on the July summer academy and to ask two questions about accommodation.
My name is Aigerim Serikova and my student number is 2417; I was accepted to the science group last week.
I will arrive in Warsaw on 2 July at 15:40 and I plan to travel to the campus by train.
Could you tell me whether the rooms are available from the evening of 2 July, or only from the 3rd?
I would also like to know whether bed linen is provided or whether I should bring my own.
If you need any documents before my arrival, I can send them this week.
Thank you for your help. I look forward to your reply. Yours sincerely, Aigerim Serikova.

I would also like to know …

seeds.sub: Writing to someone you half-know

seeds.goal: You can write an article for a school or student magazine: catch attention, describe the situation, give your view with examples and end with a call to the reader.
seeds.why: An article is written for strangers. That means a title that makes them stop and a first line that promises something.
seeds.ex: Dias wrote about phones in classrooms. Two teachers answered in the next issue.
seeds.read: Read the article and find one thing: what does the writer suggest doing about phones?
seeds.task: Write an article for a student magazine (130–160 words) about phones at school: a title, why the question matters, both sides with an example each, your own position and a final question to the reader.
model: Write a title that stops the reader
Should phones be banned in class? Ask the students first.
Open with a question or a fact
Last month our school collected 214 phones in one week. Nobody asked whether it changed anything.
Since September, phones must be left in a box at the door of every classroom.
Give the first side with an example
Teachers say that attention improved; in my maths group, three students who never spoke now answer questions.
Give the other side with an example
However, we also lost something: last term we used phones to record experiments and translate texts in seconds.
In my opinion the rule is right for lessons but wrong for breaks, when a phone is simply how we talk to our families.
A simple change would fix this: collect phones for the lesson and give them back at the bell.
End with a question to the reader
What would you choose: silence for six hours, or silence for forty-five minutes at a time?
phr: A simple change would fix this.
Одно простое изменение решило бы это.
Бір қарапайым өзгеріс мұны шешер еді.
sent: Last month our school collected 214 phones.
Phones must be left in a box at the door.
Teachers say that attention has improved.
Three students who never spoke now answer questions.
However, we also lost something useful.
We used phones to record experiments.
In my opinion the rule is right for lessons.
A phone is how we talk to our families.
Collect the phones and give them back at the bell.
What would you choose in our place?

The new rule changed the school day completely.
Three students who never spoke in maths now answer questions.
There is evidence that the rule works.
We used phones to record experiments and translate texts in seconds.
The rule also took something away.
ideas: A title that makes people stop
A general statement that phones are modern
An attack on the head teacher
seeds.title: A magazine article
seeds.sub: A question, an answer, a reader

seeds.goal: You can review a book or a film: summarise without spoilers, judge the strong and weak parts with evidence, and recommend it to a defined reader.
seeds.why: A review is where opinion has to earn its place: every judgement needs one detail behind it, or the reader stops trusting you.
seeds.ex: Alua's review of a novel was chosen for a city competition. The judges quoted her sentence about the ending.
seeds.read: Read the review and find one thing: who exactly does the reviewer recommend this book to?
seeds.task: Write a review of a book or film (130–160 words): the title and type, what it is about without spoilers, one strength with an example, one weakness with an example, a comparison, and who should read or watch it.
model: Name the work and its type
The Kite Runner by Khaled Hosseini is a novel about friendship and guilt.
It follows two boys in Kabul in the 1970s: one rich, one the son of a servant, and one afternoon that neither of them can undo.
Its greatest strength is the detail: the smell of the market, the sound of the kites, the exact words nobody says out loud.
Amir is not a likeable narrator, and that is why the book works: you keep reading because you want him to do better.
The last hundred pages, however, tie the story together too neatly for a book that spent three hundred pages showing how little life resolves.
It is closer to a family drama than to a war novel, although the war is always in the next room.
I would recommend it to readers who like slow, personal stories and do not need a happy ending.
Four stars out of five: uncomfortable in the way good books are.
phr: Он рассказывает о двух мальчиках, которые …
It is closer to … than to …
I would recommend it to readers who …
Я бы советовал его читателям, которые …

It follows two boys in Kabul in the 1970s.
Its greatest strength is the detail.
Amir is not a likeable narrator.

The war is always in the next room.
I would recommend it to patient readers.
I have read it twice since 2022.
The scene which stayed with me is very short.
It is closer to a family drama than to a war novel.
topics: The smell of the market, the sound of the kites, the words nobody says.
The detail is where this book is strongest.
The last hundred pages resolve everything the book spent three hundred pages complicating.
The ending is the weakest part.
Readers who like slow personal stories and do not need a happy ending.
This book has a specific audience.
ideas: A full retelling including the ending
seeds.title: A book or film review
seeds.sub: Judgement supported by detail

seeds.goal: You can join an online discussion: refer to what was said, state your position, support it with an example and invite a reply.
seeds.why: A forum post has to earn attention in two lines. It also teaches you to disagree with an argument instead of a person.
seeds.ex: Nurlan's post about part-time work got 40 replies. He had quoted the previous poster and answered exactly one point.
seeds.read: Read the post and find one thing: which point from the previous poster does the writer answer?
seeds.task: Write a forum post (120–150 words) in a discussion about students working part-time: refer to the previous poster, state your position, give one example from experience, admit one point on the other side and end with a question.
model: Refer to what was said before
@Marta wrote that part-time work always damages studies. I do not think it is that simple.
In my experience, the problem is not the work itself but how many hours it takes.
I worked twelve hours a week in a café last year, and my marks went up, not down, because I stopped wasting evenings.
When you have four free hours instead of ten, you actually use them.
Admittedly, a friend of mine worked thirty hours a week and failed two subjects, so the line is real.
From what I have seen, the line is around fifteen hours: after that, something has to give.
If you are thinking about it, agree the hours in writing before you start, not after.
Has anybody here managed more than twenty hours and kept their marks?
phr: I do not think it is that simple.
Я не думаю, что всё так просто.

I do not think it is that simple.

seeds.sub: Join an argument that is already running

seeds.goal: You can continue a story from a given first sentence: build the scene, raise the tension, deliver a turn and finish in one line.
seeds.why: Exam story tasks always give you the first or last sentence. The skill is joining your story to somebody else's line invisibly.
seeds.ex: Kamila's story continued the line 'The letter had been on the table for three days.' It won the school competition.
seeds.read: Read the story and find one thing: what was actually in the letter?
seeds.task: Continue this story in 130–160 words: 'The letter had been on the table for three days.' Build the scene, raise the tension, deliver one turn and finish with a single short sentence.
model: The letter had been on the table for three days.
Nobody in our flat walked past it without slowing down, and nobody touched it.
It had my grandfather's name on it, in handwriting that my mother said she had not seen since 1994.
On the fourth morning I found my mother sitting in front of it with her coat still on.
She opened it while I was standing in the doorway, read four lines and started to laugh.
It was from her brother, who had emigrated and had not written for twenty-nine years, and it contained one photograph and a bus timetable.
He was arriving on Thursday. He had assumed we still lived at the old address.
We cleaned the flat for three days.
phr: It had … on it, in handwriting that …
On the fourth morning I found …
She read four lines and started to …
Она прочитала четыре строки и начала …
It was from her brother, who …
Оно было от её брата, который …
We cleaned the flat for three days.
Nothing was the same after that.
sent: The letter had been on the table for three days.
Nobody touched it or moved it.
It had my grandfather's name on it.
My mother had not seen that handwriting since 1994.
On the fourth morning I found her in the kitchen.
She opened it while I was standing in the doorway.
It was from her brother, who had emigrated in 1994.
He had assumed we still lived at the old address.
We cleaned the flat for three days.
topics: Nobody walked past the table without slowing down, and nobody touched the envelope.
For three days the letter changed how we moved through the flat.
She read four lines and started to laugh, still wearing her coat.
The moment she opened it was not what I expected.
One photograph, a bus timetable and a brother arriving on Thursday.
The envelope held less and more than we thought.
ideas: A scene the reader can see
A detail that becomes important later
Three separate stories in one text
An explanation of the moral at the end
seeds.title: A story from a first line
seeds.sub: Continue a story that has already started

seeds.goal: You can give written advice: show you understood the problem, give two or three suggestions with reasons, warn about one risk and leave the decision to them.
seeds.why: Advice that starts with 'you must' is ignored. Advice that starts with 'in your place I would' is read to the end.
seeds.ex: Aizhan answered a pen-friend who was afraid of speaking in class. Her friend used two of the three suggestions.
seeds.read: Read the letter and find one thing: which suggestion does the writer think is the most important?
seeds.task: Write a letter of advice (120–150 words) to a friend who is afraid of speaking English in class: show you understand, give three suggestions with reasons, warn about one thing and leave the choice to them.
model: Thanks for your letter. I know exactly the feeling you describe: the sentence is ready in your head and the lesson moves on without you.
Give the first suggestion with a reason
The first thing I would do is prepare two sentences before every lesson, because it is much easier to say something you have already said in your head.
Secondly, try answering the easy questions first; nobody remembers who answered, but your voice stops being new in the room.
You could also record yourself for two minutes a day — the first week is horrible and the third week is not.
If you only do one of these, do the first one: preparation removes most of the fear.
One thing I would avoid is comparing yourself with the two students who lived abroad — that comparison teaches you nothing.
You know your class better than I do. Tell me what you decide. Aizhan.
phr: I know exactly the feeling you describe.
The first thing I would do is …
If I were you, I would …
… because it is much easier to …
One thing I would avoid is …
You know your class better than I do.
Ты знаешь свой класс лучше меня.

The sentence is ready and the lesson moves on.

Try answering the easy questions first.

If you only do one thing, do the first.

ideas: A long story about my own school year

seeds.sub: Help without deciding for them

seeds.goal: You can ask for permission in writing: say exactly what you want, why, what you have arranged already and how you will cover what you miss.
seeds.why: Permission is granted when the reader sees no work for themselves. Your job is to answer their objections before they raise them.
seeds.ex: Yerlan asked to miss two days for a competition. He listed how he would catch up, and the permission came back in an hour.
seeds.read: Read the email and find one thing: how does Yerlan plan to catch up on the lessons?
seeds.task: Write an email asking permission to miss two school days for a competition (120–150 words): what you are asking for, the dates, why it matters, what you have arranged, how you will catch up and a polite closing.
model: Say exactly what you ask for
I am writing to ask for permission to miss school on 14 and 15 April.
I have been selected for the national robotics competition in Astana, and the two days include the travel.
This is the only qualifying round of the year, and the winning teams are offered university places.
Say what you have already arranged
I have spoken to Mr Nurpeisov, who agreed to move my physics test to 18 April.
Say how you will catch up
I will take the homework for both days in advance and hand it in on Wednesday morning.
My parents know about the trip and can confirm it if you need.
Thank you for considering this. Yours sincerely, Yerlan Aitmukhambetov, 10A.

seeds.sub: Ask, justify, remove the objection

seeds.goal: You can report on a survey: state the aim, describe the method, give the main findings with numbers, and end with one recommendation.
seeds.why: A report is the first genre with headings and no emotion. Learning to hold your opinion until the last paragraph is the point.
seeds.ex: Aida's report on canteen queues used four numbers. The school changed the break timetable because of it.
seeds.read: Read the report and find one thing: what is the main recommendation?
seeds.task: Write a short report (130–160 words) about a survey among students on the school canteen: the aim, the method, three findings with numbers, one problem and one recommendation.
model: State the aim of the report
The aim of this report is to present students' views on the school canteen and to suggest one change.
A questionnaire of six questions was given to 120 students of classes 8 to 11 during one week in March.
Seventy-two per cent of students said that the queue is the main problem, not the food.
On average, students wait eleven minutes, which leaves nine minutes to eat in a twenty-minute break.
Only 18 per cent said the prices were too high, and almost nobody criticised the quality of the meals.
The data suggest that the canteen has a scheduling problem rather than a catering problem.
It is recommended that classes 8 and 9 take their break ten minutes earlier than classes 10 and 11.
If this were introduced, the queue would be divided in two without any additional cost.

Seventy-two per cent of students said …

seeds.goal: You can write about a problem where you live: describe it with evidence, explain who it affects, propose a realistic solution and answer one objection.
seeds.why: Complaining is easy; proposing is what gets published. This is the structure of every opinion piece you will read.
seeds.ex: Bekzat wrote about missing pavements in his district. A local deputy answered the article publicly.
seeds.read: Read the article and find one thing: what solution does the writer propose?
seeds.task: Write an article (130–160 words) about a problem in your city: describe it with one concrete detail, say who it affects, give evidence, propose one realistic solution, answer one objection and end with a call to action.
model: The road between the new flats on Zheltoksan Street and school number 66 has no pavement at all.
Every morning around three hundred children walk on the edge of the road while cars pass at fifty kilometres an hour.
It affects the youngest ones most: the first-classes walk this road without adults from October.
There were two accidents last winter, both in the same two hundred metres, according to the district police report.
The cheapest solution is not a new pavement but a temporary barrier and a speed limit of thirty during school hours.
Some will say that there is no money in the budget; a barrier of this kind costs less than the road repair carried out on the same street in June.

seeds.goal: You can apply for a course, a camp or a volunteer place: say what you apply for, why you, what you have done and what you would bring.
seeds.why: An application answers one question the reader never asks out loud: why should this place go to you and not to somebody else?
seeds.ex: Madina applied for a volunteer summer camp. Her paragraph about teaching her cousin to read got her the place.
seeds.read: Read the letter and find one thing: what experience does Madina offer?
seeds.task: Write an application letter (130–160 words) for a volunteer summer programme: what you apply for and where you saw it, why you want it, your relevant experience, what you would bring, your availability and a closing.

seeds.goal: You can summarise a text: name the source and topic, give the main claim, the two main supporting points and the conclusion — without adding your own opinion.
seeds.why: A summary is the hardest short genre: nothing may be invented, nothing important may be lost, and none of it may be copied word for word.
seeds.ex: Nurbek summarised a science article for his class. The teacher used the summary instead of the original for the discussion.
seeds.read: Read the summary and find one thing: what is the main claim of the original article?
seeds.task: Write a summary (110–140 words) of an article about sleep and teenagers: name the source and topic, the main claim, two supporting points, the conclusion — and no opinion of your own.
model: Name the source and the topic
The article 'Why teenagers cannot sleep early', published in a popular science magazine in 2023, examines the sleep patterns of people between 13 and 19.
Its central claim is that late sleep in teenagers is biological rather than a matter of discipline.
The author reports that the release of melatonin in adolescents begins around two hours later than in adults.
She also cites a study of 4,000 students in which a later school start time improved test results by nine per cent.
The article acknowledges that screen use makes the problem worse, but argues that it is not the cause.
It concludes that changing school timetables would be more effective than telling teenagers to go to bed.
State any limit the article names
The author notes that her evidence comes mainly from northern European schools.

Its central claim is that late sleep is biological.
The author reports that melatonin arrives two hours later.
She cites a study of 4,000 students.
A later start time improved test results by nine per cent.
The article acknowledges that screens make it worse.
It concludes that timetables should change.
The evidence comes mainly from northern Europe.
The study which she cites lasted three years.
The author does not discuss adult sleep.

seeds.goal: You can write a blog post about a trip: set the scene, tell one day in detail, give practical information and end with honest advice.
seeds.why: Travel blogs live on detail and honesty. A post that says 'it was amazing' is invisible; a post with a price and a mistake is read to the end.
seeds.ex: Sanzhar's post about a two-day trip to Turkestan was shared by a travel page with 40,000 readers.
seeds.read: Read the post and find one thing: what mistake does the writer admit making?

model: Say where and when you went
I spent two days in Turkestan in October, when the heat had finally gone.
The night train from Almaty arrives at six in the morning, which sounds terrible and is actually the best part.
By seven I was standing alone in front of the mausoleum with the light still low, and for forty minutes there was nobody else there.
The brickwork changes colour three times as the sun rises; photographs at nine look like a different building.
The entrance is free, a guide costs 4,000 tenge for a group, and the museum next door opens only at ten.
My mistake was booking a hotel in the new town: everything worth seeing is within one kilometre of the old centre.
Eat at the small place opposite the bus station rather than the restaurants at the entrance — the same food, half the price.
Go in October, stay one night, and set an alarm for half past five. That is the whole trip.

seeds.goal: You can write about a housing problem: describe it precisely, say how long it has lasted, refer to the agreement and ask for a specific action with a date.
seeds.why: Housing emails are where politeness and firmness meet. Precise dates and references are what turn a request into an obligation.
seeds.ex: Ainur's email about a broken boiler was answered in a day: she had named the date, the contract clause and a deadline.
seeds.read: Read the email and find one thing: what deadline does the writer set?
seeds.task: Write an email to a landlord (120–150 words) about a problem in your flat: what the problem is, since when, what you have already done, what the agreement says, what you ask for and by when.

seeds.goal: You can write instructions for a task: what it is for, what is needed, numbered steps, one warning and what to do if something goes wrong.
seeds.why: Instructions are tested by use, not by opinion. Writing them teaches you to imagine a reader who knows nothing.
seeds.ex: Yerkebulan wrote instructions for handing in homework on a new platform. Support requests in his class fell to zero.
seeds.read: Read the instructions and find one thing: what should you do if the upload fails?

These instructions explain how to hand in homework on the school platform.
You need your school login, the file in PDF format and about five minutes.

seeds.goal: You can apologise formally: state what happened, take responsibility without excuses, explain briefly, say what you will do to repair it and how you will prevent it.
seeds.why: Formal apologies fail when they explain too much. The order — sorry, responsibility, repair — is what makes them work.
seeds.ex: Damir apologised to a partner school after his team missed an online meeting. The partnership continued.
seeds.read: Read the letter and find one thing: what does the writer promise to prevent a repeat?
seeds.task: Write a formal apology (120–150 words) for missing an important meeting or deadline: state what happened, take responsibility, explain briefly, say how you will repair it, how you will prevent a repeat and close.
model: I am writing to apologise for our absence from the online meeting on 12 April.
The mistake was entirely ours: I had written the wrong time in our team calendar and nobody checked it.
The time difference was clearly stated in your invitation, so there is no reason to blame the schedule.
I understand that six people waited for twenty minutes and that the agenda had to be moved to next week.
Say how you will repair it
We have already prepared the presentation we owed you and can send it today, before the new meeting.
Say how you will prevent a repeat
From now on every meeting will be entered by two people, and I will confirm the time in writing 24 hours before.
Please accept my apologies once again. Yours sincerely, Damir Yesenov.

I had written the wrong time.

We have already prepared the presentation.
Every meeting will be entered by two people.
I will confirm the time twenty-four hours before.
Please accept my apologies once again.

seeds.goal: You can recommend a person: say how you know them, what they are good at with evidence, one honest limitation and a clear final judgement.
seeds.why: Recommendations without evidence are worthless — everyone is 'hard-working'. One concrete example is worth ten adjectives.
seeds.ex: Aliya's recommendation of a classmate for a volunteer post was accepted because it named a specific event and a number.
seeds.read: Read the note and find one thing: what evidence does the writer give for the person's reliability?
seeds.task: Write a note recommending a classmate for a volunteer position (120–150 words): how you know them, two strengths with evidence, one honest limitation, who they would suit and a final judgement.
model: Say how you know the person
I have studied in the same class as Alisher Turgunov for four years and worked with him on two school projects.
Give the first strength with evidence
He is genuinely reliable: during the winter charity week he came in at seven every morning for six days to open the collection point, and nobody had to remind him.
He is also good at explaining things simply, which is why the maths teacher asks him to help the younger groups.
Last year he tutored four students, and three of them moved up a grade.
He is less comfortable speaking in front of large groups, and he will avoid it if he can.
He would suit a role with small groups and regular responsibility rather than public presentation.
I recommend him without reservation for the tutoring programme. Aliya Serik, class 11B.

He would suit a role with …
Please contact me if you need more.
Свяжитесь со мной, если нужно больше.

seeds.goal: You can describe how a process works: name it, break it into stages, use sequence markers and the passive, and say what happens at the end.
seeds.why: Process description is the backbone of academic and technical writing, and it is where the passive voice finally makes sense.
seeds.ex: Askar described how tap water reaches a flat for a science project. The teacher used the text as a model of sequencing.
seeds.read: Read the description and find one thing: what happens to the water in the third stage?
seeds.task: Describe a process you understand (120–150 words): what the process is, how many stages it has, each stage in order with sequence markers, one detail that surprises people, and what the result is.
model: This is how drinking water reaches a flat in a large city.
Say how many stages there are
The process has four main stages and takes between one and three days.
First, water is taken from a river or a reservoir and passed through metal screens which remove leaves and rubbish.
It is then mixed with a chemical that makes small particles stick together and sink to the bottom of large tanks.
After that, the water is filtered through sand and gravel, which removes almost everything the tanks left behind.
Finally, a small amount of chlorine is added so that the water stays safe in the pipes.
What surprises most people is that the pipes, not the plant, are the weak point: a break in an old pipe undoes all four stages.
The result is water that is safe to drink but never completely tasteless.
sent: The process has four main stages.
Water is taken from a river or a reservoir.
It is passed through metal screens.
The screens remove leaves and rubbish.
The water is then filtered through sand and gravel.
A small amount of chlorine is added at the end.
The pipes, not the plant, are the weak point.
A break in an old pipe undoes all four stages.
The whole process takes between one and three days.
The result is water which is safe to drink.
topics: Screens first, then chemicals and tanks, then sand, then chlorine.
The four stages always run in the same order.
Sand and gravel remove almost everything the tanks left behind.
The third stage does most of the real cleaning.
A break in an old pipe undoes all four stages at once.
The weakest point is not in the plant.

seeds.goal: You can state an opinion and defend it: make one claim, support it with two reasons and an example, answer the strongest objection and close.
seeds.why: Most opinion texts fail because they say four things weakly instead of one thing strongly. Holding a single claim is the skill.
seeds.ex: Dana's post about homework was reposted by a teachers' group precisely because it argued one point only.
seeds.read: Read the post and find one thing: what objection does the writer answer?
seeds.task: Write an opinion post (120–150 words) on whether homework should be limited: one clear claim, two reasons, one example, an answer to the strongest objection and a closing line.
model: Homework should be limited to one hour a day, and the limit should be a school rule, not a wish.
The first reason is arithmetic: seven subjects times twenty minutes is already more than two hours for a fourteen-year-old.
The second is that unlimited homework punishes exactly the students who need help, because the slower you are, the longer it takes.
In my class, the students who copy the answers in the morning are not lazy; they are the ones who worked until midnight and gave up.
The strongest argument against a limit is that some subjects genuinely need practice, especially maths.
But a limit does not remove practice: it forces teachers to choose the twenty exercises that matter instead of setting fifty.
Admittedly, exam years may need an exception, and that exception should be written down too.
A rule that fits on one line would change more than another discussion about motivation.

A rule of one line would change more than a discussion.

seeds.goal: You can answer an invitation: thank the sender, accept or refuse clearly, deal with the practical details and close warmly.

I am very glad to accept, and my brother Alisher would like to come as well, if there is a place for him.

seeds.goal: You can answer a published article: name it, agree or disagree with a specific claim, give evidence from your own context and end with a demand or a question.
seeds.why: This genre teaches you to argue with a text rather than a person, and to write for an audience that has read something else.

The author is right about the numbers, but wrong about the reason.
She argues that families leave villages because the schools are weak.

It is true that no ministry can staff every village, but a teacher who works online for three schools costs less than a school bus that runs for six years.
The regional department should publish, once a year, which subjects are actually taught in every rural school.
Parents can only act on information they are given. Yours faithfully, Askar Serikbayev, Uzynagash.

seeds.goal: You can write a personal statement: say what you want to study, how the interest started, what you have done about it and what you want to do next.
seeds.why: A personal statement is judged on evidence, not enthusiasm. 'I love physics' proves nothing; 'I rebuilt a broken speaker' proves something.
seeds.ex: Zhanel's statement about biology described one experiment that failed. The admissions tutor mentioned it at the interview.
seeds.read: Read the statement and find one thing: what did the writer actually do outside school?
seeds.task: Write a personal statement (130–160 words) for a course you want to study: what you want to study, how the interest began, evidence of what you have done, what you learned from a difficulty and what you want next.
model: Say what you want to study
I am applying to study biology, and specifically the biology of soil.
The interest started with a failure: two years ago I tried to grow tomatoes on our balcony and lost every plant in three weeks.
Say what you did about it
Instead of buying new soil, I read about nitrogen, borrowed a pH test from the school laboratory and tested six samples from different parts of our district.
Four of them were far more acidic than anything the internet had promised, which explained the tomatoes and taught me not to trust a general answer to a local question.
Since then I have kept a soil notebook, and last spring I helped two neighbours change what they plant.
At school my strongest subjects are biology and chemistry, and I chose a project on composting rather than an easier topic.
The hardest part has been statistics: I can collect data much faster than I can interpret it, and that is exactly what I want to fix at university.
I would like to work on soil restoration in Kazakhstan, where the questions are local and the answers are not yet written.

seeds.goal: You can review a course or a service you paid for: describe what it was, what worked, what did not, who it suits and whether it was worth the cost.
seeds.why: The reader of this genre wants one thing: should I pay for this? Every sentence has to help them decide.
seeds.ex: Miras reviewed an online course honestly, including the price. His review is still the top comment two years later.
seeds.read: Read the review and find one thing: who does the writer say should not take this course?

model: Say what it was and what it cost
I took a twelve-week online course in academic writing, 45,000 tenge, two evenings a week.
Each week there was a ninety-minute live session, one written task and individual feedback within three days.
Say what worked, with an example
The feedback was the real product: my first essay came back with fourteen comments, and eleven of them were about structure rather than grammar.
The tutor answered questions between sessions, which for an online course is unusual and worth paying for.
The live sessions were less useful: thirty people in one room means you speak for two minutes and listen for eighty-eight.
It suits people who already write and want to write better, especially before a university application.
It does not suit beginners: two students left in week three because the tasks assumed a solid B1.

For the feedback alone, it was worth the money; for the group sessions, I would not pay half of it.

seeds.goal: You can write a story whose ending forces the reader to re-read the beginning: plant a detail, mislead honestly and reveal in one line.
seeds.why: A twist is not a trick: everything must be visible from the start. Writing one teaches you how much a reader assumes.
seeds.ex: Aisha's story about a phone call won a competition because the twist was in a detail from the second sentence.
seeds.read: Read the story and find one thing: which detail in the beginning becomes important at the end?
seeds.task: Write a story with a twist (140–170 words): plant one detail early, build a situation the reader thinks they understand, and reveal in the last two lines that they were reading it wrong.
model: My grandmother has called me at exactly seven every Sunday for eleven years, and she has never once said hello.
She starts with the weather in the village, moves to her neighbours, and finishes with a question about my studies.
I answer in the same order every week, and I have learned to cook while she talks.
Last Sunday the phone rang at seven and there was nobody on the line — only the sound of a room.
I said her name four times, then stopped and listened to the clock and a dog somewhere behind the house.
I called my uncle, who lives forty minutes from her, and he drove there without finishing his sentence.
He found her in the kitchen with the phone in her hand, laughing: she had wanted to know whether I would notice the silence.
She has never once said hello. She wanted to be sure I was still listening.

seeds.goal: You can write after an interview or a meeting: thank them, refer to one specific thing that was said, add what you forgot and restate your interest briefly.

seeds.goal: You can invite people to a longer event: give the purpose, the programme with times, the practical details and what you need from them.
seeds.why: For anything longer than two hours, guests need a timetable. Without one, half of them arrive for the part that is already over.
seeds.ex: Aigul's invitation to an open day included a fifteen-minute programme. Attendance doubled from the year before.
seeds.read: Read the invitation and find one thing: what happens at half past five?
seeds.task: Write an invitation with a programme (120–150 words) for a school open day: the purpose, who it is for, the programme with times, the practical details, what to bring and how to confirm.

seeds.goal: You can describe how you learned a skill: where you started, what did not work, what did, how long it took and what you would tell a beginner.
seeds.why: This is the most useful thing you can write for another learner — and the genre punishes vague claims like 'practice makes perfect'.
seeds.ex: Yerkin wrote about learning to touch-type. Three classmates copied his method exactly and two of them stuck to it.
seeds.read: Read the text and find one thing: what method finally worked?
seeds.task: Write about how you learned a skill (130–160 words): where you started, what did not work and why, what finally worked, how long it took, and one piece of advice for a beginner.
model: Name the skill and the starting point
Two years ago I typed with two fingers and looked at the keyboard for every word.
I started learning to touch-type because an essay was taking me three hours, and two of them were typing.
The first thing I tried was a typing game, which was fun for four evenings and taught me almost nothing.
The game rewarded speed, so I kept using the two fingers I already had and simply moved them faster.
What finally worked was boring: fifteen minutes a day of the same eight letters, with my hands under a towel so that I could not look.
It took six weeks to get back to my old speed, and four months to double it.
The hardest part was the first three weeks, when everything I wrote took twice as long as before.
If you are starting, cover your hands and accept three bad weeks: the method that feels slowest is the only one that changes anything.
